title: Rising Marks
statement: A student's quiz marks are listed in chronological order in the array marks. A rising run is a selection of quizzes, kept in chronological order, whose marks strictly increase from one selected quiz to the next; the selected quizzes do not need to be consecutive. Return the length of the longest rising run. An empty list has a longest run of 0.

examples.explanation: One longest run is 2, 3, 6, 9 with length 4. No run of length 5 exists.
Marks never rise, so any single quiz is the longest run.

hints.content: Choosing for each quiz whether to include it gives 2^n selections, far too many to test.
Define best[i] as the longest run that ends exactly at quiz i; it is one more than the best run ending at an earlier, lower mark.
That quadratic table is a solid answer; the next idea is to avoid re-scanning earlier quizzes.
Keep, for each run length, the smallest possible mark that can end a run of that length; those values are increasing.
Each new mark either extends the longest run or replaces the first stored mark that is not smaller, which binary search finds.

testCases.explanation: One longest run is 2, 3, 6, 9 with length 4. No run of length 5 exists.
Marks never rise, so any single quiz is the longest run.
A single quiz is a run of length 1.
Strictly increasing marks give a run of the whole list.
Equal marks do not rise, so the answer is 1.

solutions.title: Try every selection
solutions.intuition: Each quiz is either included in the run or skipped, and inclusion is only allowed when its mark beats the last included mark.
solutions.approach: Recurse over quizzes with the last chosen mark as state. At each quiz, take the better of skipping it and, when allowed, including it.
solutions.pseudocode: longest(i, last): if i == n return 0; best = longest(i+1, last); if marks[i] > last: best = max(best, 1 + longest(i+1, marks[i])); return best.
commonMistakes: Allowing equal marks to extend the run.
Forgetting the skip branch, which forces every quiz into the run.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The include-or-skip recursion is exponential. A table indexed by the ending quiz is quadratic, and the patience-style tail array with binary search gets to n log n by only remembering the smallest ending mark for each run length.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: For [5, 2, 8, 6, 3, 6, 9, 7], the recursion tries including 5 or skipping it, and so on for every quiz.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Among all selections, 2, 3, 6, 9 has length 4 and none has length 5.

solutions.title: Longest run ending at each quiz
solutions.intuition: A run ending at quiz i is a run ending at some earlier quiz with a lower mark, extended by one.
solutions.approach: For each quiz, look at every earlier quiz with a strictly lower mark and take the longest run ending there plus one. The answer is the largest table entry.
solutions.pseudocode: best[i] = 1; for each i: for each j < i with marks[j] < marks[i]: best[i] = max(best[i], best[j] + 1); return max(best) or 0.
commonMistakes: Returning best[n-1] instead of the maximum over all entries.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The quadratic table is the standard first dynamic-programming answer and is easy to justify. When n is large, the tails array with binary search improves it to n log n.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: The largest entry is 4, at the quiz with mark 9 or the one with mark 7.

solutions.title: Smallest tail for each run length
solutions.intuition: Among all runs of a given length, only the one with the smallest ending mark matters for future extension, and those smallest ends are increasing with the length.
solutions.approach: Maintain tails where tails[k] is the smallest mark ending a run of length k + 1. For each mark, binary search the first tail that is not smaller and overwrite it, or append when every tail is smaller. The length of tails is the answer.
solutions.pseudocode: tails = []; for each mark: k = first index with tails[k] >= mark (or tails.length); tails[k] = mark; return tails.length.
commonMistakes: Using <= in the search, which lets equal marks extend a run.
Reading tails as the actual run; it only records lengths, not a valid sequence.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I keep the smallest possible ending mark for every run length. A new mark that exceeds all tails starts a longer run; otherwise it replaces the first tail that is at least as large, which keeps future extensions as easy as possible. The tails array is sorted, so each update is a binary search, giving n log n overall. Its length is the answer even though its contents are not necessarily a real run.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: 9 appends to give [2, 3, 6, 9]; 7 replaces 9 to give [2, 3, 6, 7].

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: The length of tails is 4, which is the longest rising run.
